title: Coffee then and now (History of coffee)
sourceHeading: Coffee Then and Now (A History of Coffee)

source.filename: Practice 171 - IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 2.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Coffee was first discovered in East Africa, in an area now known as Ethiopia. A popular legend refers to a goat herder by the name of Kaldi, who observed his goats acting unusually friskily after eating berries from a bush. Curious about this phenomenon, Kaldi tried eating the berries himself. He found that these berries gave him renewed energy.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: News of this energy-laden fruit quickly spread throughout the region. Coffee berries were transported from Ethiopia to the Arabian Peninsula, and were first cultivated in what is now Yemen. Coffee remained a secret in Arabia before spreading to Turkey and then to the European continent via Venetian merchants.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Coffee was first eaten as food, though people in Arabia later made a drink by boiling the beans for their narcotic effects and medicinal value. For a time, coffee was known by Muslims as ‘Arabian wine’ because Islam forbade alcohol. Only later, probably by accident in Turkey, was it discovered that roasting the beans could produce a delicious drink. The roasted beans were first crushed and then boiled in water, creating a crude version of the beverage we enjoy today. The first coffeehouses were opened in Europe in the seventeenth century and in 1675, the Viennese established the habit of refining the brew by filtering out the grounds, sweetening it, and adding a dash of milk.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: If you were to explore the planet for coffee, you would find about 60 species of coffee plants growing wild in Africa, Malaysia, and other regions. But only about ten of them are actually cultivated. Of these ten, two species are responsible for almost all the coffee produced in the world: Coffea Arabica and Coffea Canephora (usually known as Robusta). Because of ecological differences among the various coffee-producing countries, both types have undergone many mutations and now exist in many subspecies.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Although wild plants can reach 10–12 metres in height, cultivated plants reach a height of around four metres. This makes harvesting easier and cultivation more economical. The flowers are white and smell sweet, like Spanish jasmine. Flowers give way to a dark-red berry. At first sight, the fruit is like a big cherry both in size and in colour. The berry is coated with a thin, red film (epicarp) containing a white, sugary mucilaginous flesh (mesocarp). Inside the pulp are the seeds in the form of two beans joined along their flat surfaces. The beans are in turn coated with a kind of resistant golden-yellow parchment (called the endocarp). Beneath the parchment, each bean is covered by another very thin, silvery film. The bean is bluish green verging on bronze, and is at most 11 millimetres long and 8 millimetres wide.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Coffee plants need special conditions to give a satisfactory crop. The climate needs to be hot and wet, or warm and temperate, between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, with frequent rains and temperatures ranging from 15 to 25°C. The soil should be deep and permeable, well irrigated and have well-drained subsoil. The best land is the hillsides or newly cleared woodland. The ideal altitude is between 600 and 1,200 metres, though some varieties thrive at 2,000–2,200 metres. Careful cultivation is needed to protect the plants at every stage of growth. Sowing should be in sheltered nurseries from which, after about six months, the seedlings should be moved to plantations during the rainy season, where they are interplanted with other species to shield them from wind and excessive sunlight. Only when the plant is five years old can it be relied upon to give a regular yield. A regular yield ranges from 400 grams to two kilos of arabica beans per plant and from 600 grams to two kilos of robusta beans.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Harvesting time depends on geography and therefore varies greatly among producing countries. First, the ripe beans are picked from the branches. Pickers can selectively pick approximately 250 to 300 pounds of coffee cherries a day. At the end of the day, the pickers bring their heavy hessian bags to pulping mills where the coffee cherries can be pulped (or wet milled). The pulped beans then rest, covered in pure rainwater to ferment overnight. The next day the wet beans are spread by hand across the drying floor to be sun-dried. This drying process takes from one to two weeks depending on the number of sunny days available. To make sure they dry evenly, the beans need to be raked many times during this period. Two weeks later the sun-dried beans, now called parchment, are scooped up, bagged and taken to be milled. Huge milling machines then remove the parchment and silver skin, producing green beans suitable for roasting. The green beans are roasted according to customers’ specifications and, after cooling, are packaged and sent to customers.
